source.title: Low-Rank Key Value Attention
source.authors: James O'Neill; R. Clancy; Mariia Matskevichus; Fergal Reid

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out pretraining loss across attention architectures and reports a pretraining-loss/downstream-performance correlation, but it does not fit or test the scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out FineWeb-Edu loss at multiple model scales and training budgets, but does not fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or sweep parameter/token allocations to find a compute optimum; these are not rows for V1–V3 or V7. It compares attention mechanisms and LRKV ranks at nominal base-architecture scales, relevant to V4, and reports downstream benchmark results and a correlation with pretraining BPB, relevant to V6. The reported loss curves and compute milestones are not treated as power-law results. Cited scaling-law findings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study directly examines V6 through a pretraining-loss/downstream-score correlation and evaluations at several model scales. It does not test power-law forms or compute-optimal allocation. Its architecture comparisons do not hold total parameter count fixed, as V4 requires.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the central conclusion: LRKV achieves the lowest reported final pretraining loss and highest combined downstream score at the evaluated scales, with reduced KV cache. The authors interpret their reported loss/downstream association as direct translation of pretraining gains into capability gains; the evidence establishes an association, not that causal explanation or universal task-level superiority. They do not establish a power-law or compute-optimal allocation law.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architectural comparison of LRKV with attention baselines, not a reproduction or fit of the original scaling-law methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Pretraining loss and cache efficiency differ by attention mechanism, LRKV residual rank, model scale, and context length; the paper reports rank-dependent loss changes and architecture-dependent downstream outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention substitutions and residual-rank ablations produce modest CE differences, but also change total parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changing KV parameterization can preserve or improve language-model loss at fixed backbone dimensions and token budget while reducing cache requirements.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and trained models will be released upon acceptance
record.problems: The study does not fit scaling laws or test extrapolation. Architecture comparisons are indexed by the parameter count of the Standard MHA base architecture, while the text states that alternate attention mechanisms reduce total parameter count. The downstream correlation is reported across attention mechanisms at 2.5B scale, not as a general predictive relationship. No uncertainty estimates are reported for these results.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or assessment over several orders of magnitude with other resources non-bottlenecking.
No small-run fit evaluated on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No search for loss-minimising parameter/token allocations at fixed compute.
No fixed-total-parameter architecture comparison; depth and width are not independently swept.
No power-law assessment in another modality or training regime; midtraining alone does not test this version.
No held-out predictive validation, general scaling function, or demonstrated transfer of predictions across training setups.
No fitted exponent or optimal-allocation sensitivity analysis, or test of power-law bending.

missing.what: Task-level exceptions obscured by combined scores: at 2.5B, LRKV HumanEval is 11.7% versus MHA's 13.4%; at 6.3B it is 12.8% versus 14.6%, despite LRKV's lower loss. At 128M, LRKV GSM8K is 0.3% versus MHA's 1.0%.
Task-level failures of monotonic improvement with scale: MQA GSM8K falls from 10.3% at 2.5B to 8.2% at 6.3B; GQA MMLU changes from 40.5% to 40.9%, while its GSM8K falls from 10.0% to 9.9%.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V4 verdicts: unmatched parameter budgets are an untested control, not a demonstrated scope limitation. Table values are generally transcribed correctly. The source contains conflicting architecture specifications, rank/cache figures, and correlation notation; these prevent treating nominal scales and cache claims as precise matched-budget evidence. The 128M-to-6.3B range is approximately 49-fold, despite the paper's description of three orders of magnitude.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or test of loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation fitted on small runs and compared with substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation analysis.

Tests attention-mechanism and LRKV-rank differences at nominal base-architecture scales; does not vary depth or width. The paper states that alternate attention mechanisms reduce total parameter count relative to the Standard MHA base architecture, so total parameters are not exactly matched.
Experiments are decoder-only language-model pretraining and supervised midtraining; no other modality or the other named training regimes are tested.

Reports downstream results after supervised midtraining and a correlation across attention mechanisms at 2.5B scale; does not establish a general predictive law across tasks, model families, or training setups.
No comparison of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or setups.

rows.subject: All attention mechanisms at 2.5B scale (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related pretraining validation BPB to combined downstream scores across attention mechanisms.
rows.note: The paper describes a strong positive correlation between lower pretraining BPB and higher downstream scores.
rows.check: The text and legend report R²=0.786, while the caption says R=0.786. Lower BPB is associated with higher scores, so the association with numerical BPB is negative. This is an in-sample association across five architectures.

relationships.condition: Combined downstream performance across five attention mechanisms at nominal 2.5B scale
relationships.reason: r46 reports R²=0.786 between better pretraining loss and higher combined score; r11–r15 and r36–r40 supply the paired results, supporting an in-sample association.
relationships.display_finding: Lower pretraining loss was associated with higher combined downstream scores, with an in-sample R² of 0.786.

relationships.condition: Combined scores from 128M to 2.5B for all mechanisms, and from 2.5B to 6.3B for MHA and LRKV
relationships.reason: r31–r40 show substantial aggregate improvements to 2.5B; r41 and r45 show further gains for MHA and LRKV, although these comparisons do not validate a predictive function.
relationships.display_finding: Combined scores improved substantially from 128M to 2.5B across mechanisms, with further gains at 6.3B for MHA and LRKV.

relationships.condition: GQA, MQA and MLA scaling from nominal 2.5B to 6.3B
relationships.reason: r37–r39 versus r42–r44 show gains of only 0.5, 0.1 and 0.0 points despite lower pretraining losses; aggregate improvement depends on architecture.
relationships.display_finding: Scaling GQA, MQA and MLA from nominal 2.5B to 6.3B yielded only 0.5, 0.1 and 0.0 points respectively despite lower pretraining losses.

relationships.condition: Pretraining loss as a downstream predictor across mechanisms at nominal 6.3B scale
relationships.reason: r18 has lower CE than r16 (2.304 versus 2.319), but r43 scores below r41 (33.4% versus 38.8%), showing that lower loss does not preserve downstream ranking across these architectures.
relationships.display_finding: At nominal 6.3B, the mechanism with cross-entropy 2.304 scored 33.4%, below the mechanism with cross-entropy 2.319 and score 38.8%.

relationships.condition: Individual downstream tasks rather than the combined score
relationships.reason: Table 2, beyond the recorded averages, shows LRKV's lower loss does not ensure better HumanEval or small-model GSM8K performance; this verdict uses the text and missing task-level rows.
relationships.display_finding: LRKV's lower loss did not ensure better HumanEval performance or better GSM8K performance in smaller models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Attention-mechanism and LRKV-rank comparisons at nominal base scales
reader_labels.reason: The reported CE differences across these architecture settings are modest overall, with LRKV frequently near or below the Standard MHA reference (r01–r30).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Interpretation of architecture comparisons as fixed-parameter evidence
reader_labels.reason: The study varies attention mechanisms and rank, not depth or width, and states that alternative mechanisms reduce total parameter count relative to the Standard MHA base architecture; exact parameter matching is therefore not established (r01–r30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested downstream evaluations after midtraining, including the 2.5B cross-architecture correlation
reader_labels.reason: The study reports downstream combined scores at three scales and a positive association between pretraining BPB and downstream score at 2.5B (r31–r46).
